utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. And may I ask the usher to escort the witness in the courtroom. Madam Registrar, may I ask you to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Thank you. As mentioned yesterday, we hope - you know how relative the word "hope" is here - to conclude as soon as possible, and then the floor would be for the Defence, just so the Defence is prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, you are prepared to continue with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand. There was no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, you are prepared to continue with your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The same information I gave you yesterday applies also today. Only one thing I didn't touch upon yesterday, may I ask you, did you contact before coming here one of the parties? We know that you gave a statement to a representative of the Prosecution the 24th of March last year. Were you ever contacted once again by the Prosecution or by a member of the Defence team in this case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Prosecution has not contacted me. The Defence has contacted me and asked me whether I would wish to give a statement as a Defence witness, and I declined that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then let us continue where we stopped yesterday. You recall that you were shown a document signed by a witness, a pseudonym was assigned to this witness, and therefore we can't discuss the name. A certificate issued by the Serbian Red Cross signed inter alia by you. The following question would be, was there a necessity before issuing such a certificate to relinquish the property in order to be able to leave Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such thing. Where I was in Trnopolje, these things did not happen. I heard that people who had been leaving the territory of Prijedor had the obligation to pay for the utilities, electricity, water, and the similar things. And as far as the relinquishing the rights to property, I didn't hear that. I don't know of such a thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So for the parties, the testimony of witnesses Q, Y, Z, and others would be wrong when they state here that they had to relinquish their property before being able to leave the Prijedor Municipality and before receiving such a receipt?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Exhibit 292 and 293. We will have now a very fast track going through a number of documents, please always the way that the English version is on the ELMO, and the B/C/S version be handed to our witness. Maybe in the meantime, you can briefly tell us the role of Mr. Curguz. You recall the second signature. You signed at the left-hand side of this document of this certificate, on the right side was Pero Curguz. What was his role?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, let me tell you that I don't know what document this is all about. I saw it yesterday actually. Mr. Curguz was a member of the team of the municipal Red Cross from Prijedor. He was not on his own. There were other people, four or five women were there with him, and Mr. Curguz was one of the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The name is redacted, because it's a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read this decision. I understand what it says here, but I didn't see here that it says the shop ceases to operate and private property. I've never done any such thing in my whole life. But let me help you, if somebody wanted to have a private shop or a private business, they had to apply for that stating the place where the business would be operating from and what activity would it be engaged in. Once is ceases to operate, obviously one also has to report that the business ceases to operate, and thus that the obligations of that company towards the state ceased to exist. As for relinquishing the right to property, I've never heard of any such thing, nor have I heard that any such decisions were issued. I can see that this was signed by Ranko Travar, the secretary for the economy. I don't know based on which he is quoting some articles of the law. But I don't think this was confiscating of property. It was just the announcement on the part of the owner that his business would cease to operate after a certain date. This is how I understand this. And it says here that the person applies for the business to cease operating. I believe that that person, as it says here, this was submitted to the -- to various institutions, so I suppose that this person was under the obligation to meet his obligations towards the various funds. I don't understand everything about this thing. These are some obligations and some commitments that a business owner had towards the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then, please, Exhibit S293. For the parties, this has to be read in conjunction with transcript 7606 through 7607. This means that I have understood this decision well. This is a certificate in which it says that the person who had obligations have met -- has met obligations towards pension funds, health fund, and so on and so forth. I can't see anywhere here that the taxes have been paid, and I don't see here that the property has been confiscated. I can see here that this business, this company, this shop or kiosk is going to cease to operate as of a certain date. I am not familiar with all this, but my logic tells me, and I assume that this is the case based on what I can read in this document. These are municipal affairs, the affairs within the purview of the municipal secretariat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you for a moment can come back to Exhibit S12. I hope it's still in this redacted version. Exhibit S12. May I first see it before it is put on the ELMO, please. Would it be please placed on the ELMO that we can see it together. We have only one version. And immediately to the signature block, please. The bottom line. Yesterday, you already tried to read this what we can see under the signature of Pero Curguz. And I omitted yesterday to go in some more details on what we can read there. I think it reads, based on the certificate of departure of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, 8 August 1992. What was this, the certificate of departure of the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what this is all about. I don't know why Pero Curguz was supposed to sign this. I never sign any other documents but those that constitute the certificate requested by the Red Cross about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people being there. I don't think this is a forgery. This is my signature. That's how I sign documents. But I don't know what this is. I don't know. I may have been told that the person was leaving the centre in Trnopolje, that maybe a member of his family came to take him, and that this certificate is supposed to be signed indicating that that person indeed had been here. I'm -- I didn't read the contents of this document, and the Red Cross has nothing whatsoever to do with the municipal authorities. This is an international organisation, so I believe that I was under the impression that I did not have to read the contents. I can see in the heading "Red Cross", and this is also the seal of the Red Cross of Prijedor. Maybe it is not nice of me to say that maybe this has been planted on me to sign. I don't know whether anybody had any ill intentions. But I really don't know why I signed this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please don't misunderstand it. You're not in any way the accused in this case. We want just to hear from you, as you sit here as a witness, to know why was it necessary that there was a certificate as we can read it of departure issued by the Autonomous Region of Krajina? What had the Autonomous Region of Krajina to do with this release?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I know that according to the logic of subordination, a Krajina should have been superior to the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. I don't know whether one was supposed to ask the Autonomous Region of Krajina permission to leave either Municipality of Prijedor or some other city. This doesn't make sense to me. A number of people were asked to pay their bills, their rent, their utilities before they left town. A number of people - I don't know how many - but starting with autumn 1991 up to spring 1992 left Prijedor in an organised manner. Muslim and Croat families, mostly women and children, were leaving, whereas able-bodied men remained in the city. I don't want to guess. I know that these things happened. Whether this is correct or not, but I don't know that the number that is mentioned is rather large. Some say that between ten and 15.000 people left Prijedor at that time by buses in an organised manner. I would like to thank you for having said that -- what you've said when you asked me this question. Yesterday all day, you act in a very fair manner and with a lot of -- I was treated by you with a lot of respect, and I would like to thank you for that. So if I need to repeat my answer, I really don't know why the autonomous province of Krajina was in the position to order anything to the municipality or ask the municipality to issue any certificates or why would a Krajina issue a certificate for somebody to leave a certain municipality? I really don't know why this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now turn to a totally different issue, and this is the work of the Prijedor Crisis Staff. May the witness please be shown Exhibit S60. Do you recall this meeting, the 15th of May? You appear --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this meeting, and I can see here that I attended this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired by Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the council.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the National Defence Council of Prijedor Municipality. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have the agenda. We don't want to waste time with the agenda, but let's go to the conclusions. First conclusion: If you could go a little bit more down, yes. Still on the first page, only at the end of the page. It was on the organisation and the functioning of the Crisis Staff. And here it reads: "The draft of the decision on the organisation and function of the Crisis Staff is approved under the proviso that a representative of the Garrison in Prijedor be added to the proposed list of members of the Crisis Staff." First, who proposed the list of members of the Crisis Staff, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see here that these are members of the Executive Board, president and the vice-president, and I can see that Vladimir Arsic was also proposed, and the person who proposed it was the president of the Municipal Assembly, Dr. Stakic. And I can see here all the persons, Rade Javoric, the commander of the staff, Cedo Sipovac was the representative of the army, Travar, Zeljaja, Kovacevic and so on and so forth. Probably it was based either on the statute of the Municipal Assembly or the provisions of the laws of the Krajina or the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was stipulated what the composition of these bodies should be, and I believe that it was based on that that Mr. Stakic put forth this proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Correct. The only question is why in addition to that what is in fact foreseen elsewhere a representative of the Garrison in Prijedor should be added to the proposed list of members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because of cooperation between the police, the army, and security organs. Slavko Budimir is here, and he is the secretary for people's defence. And he was the one to coordinate the behaviour of both the police and the army and the engagement of people, mobilisation of people. And I suppose that it had to be put in writing that a military representative should be there to participate in the discussions on dealing with these issues. As far as I remember, I attended several of these meetings, and in any of them the people -- the National Defence Council or the Crisis Staff ever issued any orders to the army, at least I don't remember. That may have happened in some other meetings that I didn't attend. But in any case, this was not possible because there was a different chain of subordination applied to the army. There was the garrison in Prijedor, and Vladimir Arsic was under the command of the Banja Luka corps on the 1st Krajina Corps. In any case, that is the same corps. Maybe the names were changed later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the implementation of this conclusion? Did, in fact, a representative of the garrison in Prijedor participate in meetings of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I attended several sessions. I don't remember that he attended every time, but sometimes Mr. Arsic was present, or Cedo Sipovac or Rajlic was there. As representatives probably, if they were supposed to resolve certain problems related to the life and work of the army. That's what I remember. I don't remember any discussion taking place about military actions because there were no military actions in town or around the town. I am certain that this is the reason because the state of war prevailed, troops went to the front line. It needed to be decided how many people should be assigned to the police to maintain law and order in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now turn to the next page, and this would be agenda points 2 and 3. "Mobilisation in the municipality and the issue of the status of deployed forces." Apparently following these minutes, you participated you in the discussion, and then the following conclusions were adopted. I'm especially interested in the following, the second: "All persons who have failed to respond to the mobilisation callups starting from 17 September 1991 may not participate in decision-making on organisation of work and security matters in companies and other legal entities. The directors of companies and other executive organs are responsible for the immediate implementation of this conclusion." Then start the transformation of both TO staffs and former unified command for control and command of all the units formed in the territory of the Municipality. Do you recall these two conclusions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not particularly, but I understand what they are all about, the people who failed to respond to their mobilisation callups should under the law be held liable. That was so however you viewed it. From the inside or from the outside. It was the official state organisation called the Serbian Republic Bosnia-Herzegovina, and those who failed to respond Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to mobilisation had to be subjected to certain measures. They certainly couldn't be engaged in work related to safeguarding facilities and installations and any works related to security. And I see that directors and managers are made responsible to make sure of that. And about the second conclusion, the headquarters of the Territorial Defence should be included in the single command. As far as I remember, it was later called the Command of the Region to avoid having several military organisations. Therefore, the staff of the Territorial Defence commanded by Rade Javoric, and the staff in which I was, which was not really a military organisation, were formally united and resubordinated to the command of the region. That is, Commander Arsic. And everything was from then on under the command of military post box 4777. Yes, here it is written. A part of the remaining conscripts should be assigned to units, blah, blah, priority to be given to the reinforcement. So this must have been a preliminary decision. I remember telling you that. And I also said that on the 16th or the 17th, I received an order to the effect that I and what was referred to as my staff and the staff of Mr. Javoric without any exceptions should be attached to the command of the region, that is, of the brigade, military postbox 4777.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So in conclusion, this would mean -- you mentioned yesterday the number of one to two thousand persons maximum. They would be from now on under the command of Mr. Arsic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know for sure actually, but I think those were the numbers within the Territorial Defence units. They were brought under the command of the brigade. And that included all the men who are military conscripts or who volunteered to serve in the army and who were not in the ranks of civilian police. So all of them were either within the composition of one or the other brigade included in this military postbox. All military conscripts from the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it would be correct that war units 4777 and 8316 would be part of the 43rd or 343rd Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the 43rd Brigade and the 343rd Brigade are one and the same thing. When they were -- when this brigade was restructured, it was also renamed into the 343rd Brigade. When that happened exactly, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This is one and the same brigade, no doubt. But these war units, 4777 and 8316 would be within this brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about this second one, 8316. I don't know which unit that is. But it's possible. If this 8316 was within the Kozara Brigade which was part of the Territorial Defence, then it would not be the case. As for the command of the region, the command of this brigade was ex officio commander of the region. The region was a broader area. Therefore, all the other brigades in that territory were under the command of the region, that is, under the command of Arsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But then also in the context of the next following, the fifth conclusion, that all conscripts who have been issued uniforms and other military equipment and who have not joined up to return their equipment as soon as possible. This is only a natural decision. But the question, please help us understand this, how is it possible that the Prijedor Municipality Crisis Staff decided in this way on issues normally being in the area of the military, and in part, the police forces?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will try to assist you on this issue. I hope you will understand. It is not the army that engaged civilians into its units. This was done through the Ministry of Defence, or rather in Prijedor, through the Secretariat of National Defence headed by Slavko Budimir. And if somebody needed to be called up, to be mobilised, then when the army saw fit to do that, it was done by the Secretariat for National Defence. They handled all affairs related to appointment, relief of duty, engagement, distribution of men, et cetera. This was done by the Secretariat for National Defence and the Crisis Staff. I don't know whether we mentioned yesterday, all men in that state who at one point had completed their military service had their military equipment at home, not including weapons, of course, unless the Territorial Defence was mobilised and people were issued with weapons. So this was a way to call upon people to return the equipment they had been given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. But in the centre of our interest is, no doubt, number 3. And this is not about conscripts but it's on the formation of a unit, here "form a unified command for control and command of all the units formed in the territory or municipality." And then wouldn't it be alone for the military to decide what priority is given? And here, the Crisis Staff indeed decides priority is to be given to the reinforcement of war unit, first of all, 4777. How could the Crisis Staff decide on these military issues?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how else to answer this question. This could have been done only through the Ministry of Defence and the Secretariat for National Defence as part of the Municipal Assembly. And all reassignments could have been handled only that way. Applications could have been made, plans could have been formulated, requests made. But only through the Secretariat for National Defence. And since this Secretariat was part of this National Defence Council and part of the Crisis Staff, it is logical that this should be discussed here. And I suppose it was formulated as a task to the Secretariat to execute this assignment. It was not something for the National Defence Council. At least, that is what I know. Maybe there could have been other provisions in the law allowing for this. I'm not a professional military person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's briefly touch upon point 4, if we could see the bottom part of this page, please. It reads: "The public security station in concert with the army command should draft the plan of disarmament, after which the actual process should be set in motion and with the assistance of the media." First, public security station in concert with the army command. How could the Crisis Staff decide on these issues?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here "conclusion." A conclusion is not an order, and it's not a decision either. This was concluded, drawn as a conclusion probably for the sake of securing the Municipality of Prijedor, namely, the disarmament of all those illegally armed paramilitary formations. I don't know how else this could have been done except by having them disarmed by the police in cooperation with the army. The weapons were supposed to be collected and taken away, with appeals made to the public to carry out this conclusion, to implement it. This is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And then let's turn to the next page, taking over of the duties of the military department, and then the conclusion: "The municipal Secretariat for National Defence is requested to prepare for the Municipal Assembly executive committee a draft staffing table for the Secretariat which shall include the tasks taken over from the military department." Which were these tasks taken over from the military department and how could the Crisis Staff or the National Defence Council better, in this case, how could the National Defence Council "take over" duties from the military department?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it's possible that some superior order resulted in a restructuring and something that was called earlier military section became part of the Secretariat for National Defence. This must have been an obligation given to the Secretariat for National Defence by the National Defence Council to formulate a categorisation of vacancies and jobs, because I told you before, calling up people to be mobilised and engaging civilians in any way into the army must have been done through a summons from the Secretariat for National Defence or as it was earlier called, the military section. The military section employed civilians, not military persons. They were tasked with issuing callups, forming and reforming units, and it is through them that the army made its applications and requests reflecting its needs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So what finally in conclusion, this conclusion Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. would mean that part of the duties of the military department were now taken over by the National Defence Council. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was the municipal Secretariat for National Defence. I'm sorry, I hastened a little. The municipal Secretariat for National Defence was given the task of preparing a categorisation of jobs and vacancies because they had taken over the purview of the former military section. And it all became part of the Secretariat for National Defence headed by Slavko Budimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes the discussion of this document. Let us now turn briefly to Documents S130 and 203. Can we please see the entire document. Do you recall having seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then it's not of assistance to go in some details. 203. Can you confirm this decision? Was this decision implemented as it reads here: "Relieved of duties as of 29 May, 1992 ..."? In your interview, maybe you hadn't this document before you, of 24 March last year, on page 11, you state: "It would be the 17th of May, 1992." To the best of your recollection, what would be the correct date?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the issuing of this decision?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Not the issuing, but as it reads here: "... is relieved of duties as of 29 May, 1992..." Is this date correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received this decision, and it corresponds to this date, that's the day when I received it. And before that, the commander of the region, in other words, the 43rd Brigade, issued an order resubordinating me to the command of the brigade, and from that moment on, I ceased to be the commander of the staff of the Serbian Territorial Defence, and I was under the command of the 43rd Brigade. What it says in this decision probably reflects the fact that when it was impossible for the staff to meet, the staff decided to relieve me of the duties of commander of Territorial Defence, and I received this decision precisely on this date, the 29th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Then it continues: "... placed under the command of the command of the region." What would this mean in terms of names, who were from now on your superiors in the hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Commander Arsic, commander of the region and commander of the 43rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And who would be the superior to Mr. Arsic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember exactly at that time who was commander of the Banja Luka Corps. I forgot the name. At the time it was the -- General Talic was chief of staff of the corps, and I forget whether the corps was called Banja Luka Corps at the time or not, or the Corps of Republika Srpska. It could have been General Vukovic. I've forgot. Or maybe General Talic was already corps commander. I really can't remember. It could easily be that General Talic was already corps commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt, your immediate superior from now on was Mr. Arsic. Did you have to change your office?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could say that since the staff did not really exist, the commander of the other staff, the TO staff, moved into the barracks together with all the staff, and all the staff. So I spent my time in that barracks all the time. And the former TO staff offices were transformed into a logistics base. And I had my ways and means of taking from there to Trnopolje cigarettes and some other supplies that I couldn't get through the Red Cross. However, I was subordinated to the command of the brigade, and I wasn't able to do anything without their approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As it would be always in wartime. You mentioned the barracks. Which barracks do you mean?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks, military postbox 4777. I believe some other military postbox numbers were also there because the military have within their organisation the so-called development command. I believe some units were under its command. The barracks held the command of the region, Commander Arsic, with all his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, did you ever see in this Zarko Zgonjanin barracks arrested or detained persons or persons being there for the purpose of interrogation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I didn't see that. You mean some detainees under interrogation or something? I never saw anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May we then turn to Exhibit Number S21, please. May it be please put on the ELMO in a way that we can see the entire document. What does it mean "the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic shall be established as an armed force of SBiH. Command and control of the Territorial Defence shall be exercised, municipal district, and regional staffs, and the republic staff of the SBiH TO"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we discussed that yesterday, was established. The Ministry of Defence Bogdan Subotic was appointed pursuant to the provisions of the constitution and the decision of the Presidency at a session which was held on the 15th of April, 1992, took the decision on the establishment of the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as an armed force of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The state was established, the authorities were established, and the Minister of Defence therefore ordered mobilisation. Before that, the immediate threat of war was proclaimed. As far as I know, the mobilisation call was published in the media and conscripts were supposed to respond to this mobilisation call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This decision was, in fact, implemented?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because this applied to the tasks of the Territorial Defence staff which existed and which was under the command of Mr. Rade Javoric. And this mobilisation was indeed carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the following documents immediately one after the other: 175, 68, 70, 69, 72, and 79. Starting, please, with 175. This is an order apparently issued by the Crisis Staff, and it reads: "Commands and members of the military and regular police forces are hereby ordered to immediately seize all materials ..." We shouldn't go into formal details. But how can the Crisis Staff of Prijedor order commands and members of the military and regular police forces to do something?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. The -- probably because at that time, there was still an order, that is, a decision, of the Presidency in place which dealt with the immediate threat of war. I suppose that the Crisis Staff did have a possibility to ask that of the police and the army in order to prevent plunder and theft. You know, such things did happen, and the way I understand it, it was asked for these illegally acquired materiel and equipment to be seized. I can see that this concerns the prevention of further plunder of private property and state property, and I can see that this also concerns the control of the exit and entry of all persons from buildings, the control of all the telephone calls. The military police did its own job, and the civilian did its own job. The times were weird, and the philosophy and the mind set of people was different. There were members of my people who carried arms, and for that reason, they thought they could do whatever they wanted to do under the guise of the military uniform or the uniform of a civilian or a military policeman. And because they wore uniforms, they thought they could seize people's property, and because there were such things, there was a need to introduce some order into town and prevent looting and threat because as I've already said, the truth is that there were such things happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned this, and it's quite understandable. But let's now turn to 3: "Residents and residents' councils are ordered to monitor around the clock the comings and goings of all people at the entrances to their apartment buildings. Any misconduct should be reported to the competent police or military organs in person or Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. by telephone ..." And then we can read two telephone numbers. "Any misconduct should be reported ..." Yesterday, we briefly touched upon some heinous crimes in Omarska, Mount Vlasic. Wouldn't it have been the obligation of everybody, each resident, be it now an ordinary civilian or be it a member of the Crisis Staff, to report any misconduct to the competent police or military organs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the case. For example, people organised their tenants' councils in building in order to deal with some minor issues, and it was asked from them to participate in all this to control the coming and going of people in their building in order to prevent the looting of property and other such misconduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Once again, to come back in case of the killing of a huge number of persons, wouldn't it be the obligation under the rules and the law of former Yugoslavia to report these killings to the competent police or military organs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably yes, unless this happened during war operations. It was provided for by the law, and this is the case in every country, and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was no exception to that rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You mentioned yesterday that related to the mass killing at Mount Vlasic, you were asked to report to -- to write a report to Mr. Arsic. Did you write that report and what happened with the report, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote the report in the brigade command. I said what I knew. Up to that time, I never heard of any such thing having happened, and I don't know who the escorts were. I know that the civilian police served as escorts. I heard that only two or three days later. They asked me to write a report on when this happened. I wrote a report to that effect, and that report remained in the brigade command. I wrote what I knew. I probably stated when this happened, when the group had left. I don't remember whether they left in two or three buses. I also stated that the transportation was organised, that the Executive Board supplied the fuel, and that the public security station provided escort for this convoy, and these escorts were tasked with providing for the security of these people until their arrival in the territory of Travnik and further on in either Bosnia and Herzegovina or abroad, depending on where people wanted to go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you still have a copy of this report in your possession?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I wrote there? No, no, I only remember what I said, and that was that regardless of when such a departure was organised, the president of the Executive Board was aware of that. He helped the organisation of this departure. Commander Arsic was also aware of this departure. Either he or somebody else from the military was supposed to inform the military structures in that part of Mount Vlasic to allow for a safe passage of these people. I believe that I wrote something to that effect. I also wrote in that statement that I didn't know about the incident and that I was not officially informed about it. I believe that I heard of the incident in the Red Cross. And after that, I was asked to draft my report or statement about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you discuss these killings in the Crisis Staff or bilaterally together with Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be honest, I really don't remember. I don't remember when this happened exactly. After the order issued by the Commander Arsic and the decision of the Crisis Staff, I stopped attending Crisis Staff meetings or any other meetings for that matter, and I really don't remember ever having discussed that with him. I probably talked about that with my acquaintances, people that I knew who were surrounding me because it was something terrible. It was an atrocious thing that happened. I may have talked about it with Dr. Stakic as well, but it was not in any formal manner, if you know what I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let us please turn to S68. Once again, we shouldn't go into the details. The question is how it's possible that the president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic, orders that it is hereby -- "An order is hereby issued to the military police organs and the organs of the Prijedor State Security Service"? It's not a request; it's an order.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that it says "order" here. Maybe the army and military police were requested to take possession of all illegally seized property from other members of the military and the military police. However, other people had done that as well, and maybe that's why it was asked from the army and the police to prevent that and that for all illegal property to be taken hold of. I heard that one of the companies in question was Velepromet. I'm not sure. I can only say that at that time there were very few people actually within that brigade, and under that command of that brigade, there were a lot of people on the strength of the civilian police. So maybe this applies more to those who wore uniforms. But it also applied to everybody. Now, what is the logic behind this order being issued by the Crisis Staff, and here it quotes Article 7 on the decision on the organisation and activities of the Crisis Staff. But I believe that this decision on the work of the Crisis Staff was passed pursuant to the constitution and laws of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I believe that pursuant to such a decision, the Crisis Staff was in the position to issue an order like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit 70, 7-0. Here we can see "Crisis Staff president" illegible, Stakic, maybe, signed and stamped. It reads: "The blockade of the town shall remain in force." Why this?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, and I know that you know, that on the 30th of May, there was a military attack on the town of Prijedor. There were a number of organised people who participated in that attack, and 16 people killed during that attack in front of the municipal building and all over the town. And I assume that the Crisis Staff expected that something like that would happen again, and that's why it asked for the blockade of the town to remain in force. The blockade was carried out by units -- or actually units under of the command of the region, together with members of the police. They set up checkpoints to control those people who were entering and leaving town. So everybody who was moving around was checked by those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So the addressee, in fact, would be the public security station or, as you mentioned, the command of the region. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit S69. Once again, issued by the Municipality of Prijedor Crisis Staff, an order to supply for the troops -- supplies for the troops shall be provided by the Zarko Zgonjanin barracks pursuant to the order issued by the commander. Could you please comment on this document. Once again, an order into the direction of the army.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- what we can see here are vehicles. For a short period of time, I issued everybody with fuel certificates, but this only lasted for a few days, and then it was the Executive Board who did that via its services, the fuel. As we know, there is a petrol station in the barracks, and fuel was issued on the order of the commander. And fuel had to be brought from somewhere. I apologise. This had to be taken from -- this had to be taken from the storage, fuel storage, in town, the so-called Energopetrol. So the fuel had first to be transported to the barracks, to petrol stations, and then it was issued in the way that is stated herein.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But one point of special interest for me is it reads, close to the end: "For Crisis Staff vehicles." What does it mean, "Crisis Staff vehicles"? Did you have special cars provided for the members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But if the Crisis Staff is mentioned, then this is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the body that in the peacetime was the Municipal Assembly and the Executive Board, secretariats, president of the Executive Board, vice-president of the Executive Board, various secretaries for the economy, for People's Defence. As far as I know, there were two or three vehicles used by the municipality officials when they went on business, when they travelled on business. So I suppose that what is meant here are these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you yourself have your own car and driver?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I was issued the order to resubordinate myself to the region command, I had a car that I got from a company. I had my own car which was an old Peugeot 305, very old. And this first car mentioned, I used it for 15 days, and then I returned it to the company that had given it to me. It was sometime around 16, 17, 18 or 20 May. I can't remember exactly. The car was given to me by the company called -- the textile company. I returned that car in good order, the way I got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you know which kind of -- which car was driven by the president of the municipality as of the 30th of April, 1992, we'll say which car was driven by Dr. Stakic and who was the driver at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but it wasn't Dr. Stakic himself who drove that car. And I also forgot what car was that. I remember that there was a blue Lada. As far as I remember, this was used by inspectors, by officials. And there was also another blue -- white car, a white Lada. The president of the municipality must have been driven in a better car, but I don't remember what car was that. It seems to me that earlier on, before all these incidents happened, the president of the municipality was driven in a black Mercedes. Now whether Dr. Stakic also used the same car, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then let's skip S72 and go immediately and finally before the break to Exhibit S79. Once again, an order issued by the president of the Crisis Staff, Dr. Milomir Stakic. An order to the Prijedor Public Security Station and the Prijedor regional command. "... are ordered to form a joint intervention platoon to be made up of 20 members from each with the basic task of preventing looting and other criminal activities in the area of the municipality and movement of all unregistered vehicles and vehicles driven by members of the army and police without regularly approved travel authorisation." So we already touched upon this, on an intervention platoon, yesterday. So apparently this intervention platoon was made up by members of the security station and the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this transpires from this order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And it reads in number 2: "That the members of the platoon shall be chosen from among the existing members of the army and the police."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: How could the Crisis Staff give such an order to army and police?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that the Article 3 and 7 on the decision of the organisation are quoted here. I don't know anything about these articles and what the contents of these articles are. But it seems that the order was based on these articles. In any case, it is well known what this is all about. I've told you already that a number of people wore uniforms, and some of them were not even on the strength of either the police or the army and still they wore uniforms because at that time, almost everyone wore a uniform. Some of them were not authorised to carry either a uniform or arms, and these people would seize other people's cars, and they would use those cars - I'm talking about both members of the police and the army - and this had to be stopped. And they -- these vehicles, if they were driven by people who were not authorised to travel, who did not have a document - I'm talking again about the military or the police members who when travelled had to have an authorisation, an official document. So if these people did not have the authorisation to drive vehicles, then it was ordered to the police and the military to take those vehicles over -- away from them. I don't know whether the Crisis Staff could issue such an order, but in any case this was ordered in order to prevent looting and to preserve the property of people. This was the justification for this order. Now, whether this order was at all possible or not, I cannot go into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But did I understand you yesterday correctly that this platoon, in fact, was implemented and this order was implemented and this intervention platoon was established; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that this order was not carried out. I don't know who members of this platoon were and who its commander was. But I don't believe that this order was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. For this part, for technical reasons we have to make a break now once again, and therefore the trial stays adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we now turn to a totally different issue. May I ask you, was there ever a discussion in the Crisis Staff or in other groups, national defence or whatsoever, on the incident in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I remember it. I suppose I know what happened, but it happened before, before that second attack took place. I think it was on the 22nd or somewhere around that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In your statement, it reads on page 45, when asked by Mr. Koumjian: "Did the Crisis Staff discuss the situation at its meetings after the killing of the men at the checkpoint?" Your answer was: "Yes, it was discussed, but the army had already `came with an ultimatum to surrender the weapons within 48 hours.' As much as I remember, that was accepted, and then it was radio broadcasted." Question: "And the radio person who actually announced the ultimatum was Dr. Stakic. Is that correct?" Answer: "Well, I don't know exactly. Maybe he was the one who signed, but I don't know if he was the one at the radio announcing it or it was, you know, radio worker, speaker." Question, "was the ultimatum given in the name of the Crisis Staff of Prijedor"? Answer: "I think. I'm not sure. It was in the name of the army." To the best of your recollection, what would be your testimony today on the events immediately before Hambarine and immediately after Hambarine, especially the involvement of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I hadn't understood the question well last year, or maybe I was confused by the whole procedure, the questions, the translations, et cetera. I don't think Dr. Stakic was the one who presented this request. It was done through the radio at somebody else's request. As far as I know, on the 22nd, an army patrol was attacked on its way to Hambarine. They were shot at from a light machine-gun. I think the person involved was Aziz Aliskovic. And throughout that time, there were problems at the checkpoint in Kozarac where passage was denied. This checkpoint was manned by Muslims from the Territorial Defence so that people had to take alternative roads to arrive in the town. I don't know whether it was on the 26th or 29th of May, but I know it was a couple of days after this incident in Hambarine, that this column was also attacked. Some of the soldiers were killed. And there followed an order or a command from the command of the region to eliminate this checkpoint and to allow free passage from Banja Luka to Prijedor. I think that was the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To come back to the first part of the question, at that time, you were asked: "Did the Crisis Staff discuss the situation at its meeting after the killing of the men at the checkpoint?" And you answered: "Yes, it was discussed." To the best of your recollection, was this issue discussed in the Crisis Staff? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is possible, but I'm not completely certain. It would have been logical to discuss it, but whether the discussion was official and to what extent the army was involved, I cannot claim with any certainty. Maybe the Crisis Staff discussed it at a meeting which I did not attend, but I don't remember it. Because this was at a time when I had ceased to be officially the commander of the TO staff and was attached to a unit of the 343rd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This was as of, as we just established a moment before, the 29th of May. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I can't remember the exact date, but it was somewhere between the 26th and the 29th of May that this incident took place on the road from Banja Luka to Prijedor, around the Kozarac intersection. It might have been on the 26th, but I can't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you yourself read out the ultimatum in the media?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't. I had nothing to do with the radio station at the time. It was only in May 1994 that according to the decision of the Executive Board, I was nominated to become manager of the radio station, and indeed, became the director.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the parties, I'm making reference to transcript page 2864 and 6808. The events in Kozarac, were they discussed in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't attend any such discussion. I suppose it was discussed. It's impossible that it shouldn't have been discussed, at least informally among people. But whether any official discussion had taken place, I don't know. As far as I'm concerned, I told you already who summoned me, in which way, and how I became involved in this general misfortune suffered by the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you mention this "misfortune suffered by the people," I think one conclusion of these orders we saw in the past, especially based on Exhibit Number S250, was that it was for the Crisis Staff to take care that the order in town was maintained or re-established. What about now these crimes committed indisputably in the camps of Omarska and Keraterm, especially the so-called Room 3 massacre? Did you committed to maintain or re-establish the order in town discuss these crimes in the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That happened during times when I had no direct link with the Crisis Staff. And I suppose this, too, must have been discussed. It was a terrible event that occurred for I don't know exactly what reason. I do know that people were detained in this Keraterm camp. I don't know what grounds and how. Rumour had it that those were people who had been involved in actions against the town. I forget now whether it was before these actions or after. I didn't know at the time who was in charge over there. I heard about it later, over the radio. I know that some sort of military attack was carried out against those people. I heard many people were killed. But I don't know the real reason why this ugly incident occurred. Although you could hardly call something like that an "incident"; it is a crime committed by men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be your testimony that the fact that these crimes were committed, both in Keraterm and Omarska, were public knowledge in town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think they were. They could have become later. People knew about the crime in Keraterm. And what I said before, I said in reference to Omarska, because that camp was not far from the town, and the shooting must have been heard. I don't know where I was at the time. The event took place in the evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: For the transcript, it reads "Omarska, it was not far from town." Did you really want to say Omarska, or did you want to say Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People knew about what happened in Keraterm. And as far as Omarska was concerned, it was some sort of investigative prison. And I don't think people knew what was going on in there. It fell within the competence of the Secretariat for Internal Affairs, the public security station. And it was the late Simo Drljaca who was chief of the police station. I don't know on whose orders this centre was established and those investigations were carried out. The rest of it, I know about from what I saw on television, just like other people, and I listened to statements made by people who had been detained there and realised then that lots of things had been going on in there. I don't think those things should have happened. I don't think that is in our spirit and culture as a nation. I don't know how to explain it. I don't think it should have happened at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did anybody in the Crisis Staff try to take action to prevent that something like this would happen again in the future? Were there any investigations? Were there any reports to the responsible authorities, be it in the military area or be it in the police or public prosecutor or area of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was discussed by the Crisis Staff. I didn't hear or witness any such discussion. But I suppose it couldn't have gone unnoticed. If the Crisis Staff made decisions regarding water, food, mobilisation, traffic control, requisition of vehicles, et cetera, I don't think they would have omitted to require reports about all these events, and they probably required an investigation by the courts, because from what I know, the incident in Keraterm involved civilians. And civilians are in charge of -- civilians are the responsibility of civilian authorities, and I suppose something of that kind must have been requested or even demanded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did anybody of you ever go to Keraterm or Omarska and to find out what are the real facts behind that what happened?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have said already I had never been to Omarska or Keraterm. I know that Mr. Simo Drljaca and others used to go there, and I know that every day, one doctor and one male nurse would go there to visit, and it is from them that I heard that people from the police went there, including Mr. Simo Drljaca. Whether he had taken some measures to prevent unwarranted action by the police, I don't know. I never read any reports to that effect and never heard anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You just stated that "Mr. Simo Drljaca and others used to go there." Who were these others?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose his associates or his subordinates in the chain of command of the public security centre, that is, the Secretariat of the Interior in Prijedor. Later, I saw some footage on television depicting those men, which means that television crews and journalists also visited the camps. I don't know exactly what this footage shows. I don't remember any more, but I know that television crews must have been there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In 1992, and I really ask you this question related to 1992 and from your perspective, if possible, of 1992, starting with the 7th of January, 1992, who was the most important politician in the municipality of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. The government that was established in the night of the 29th and 30th of April consisted of the top leaders of the party and municipality. From January that year until the 30th of April, we had the government that was elected at the elections. It was only formal and had no practical power. From the 29th of April onwards, however, the supreme body in the municipality was the assembly, and later the Crisis Staff, and later the War Presidency. When things calmed down a little, I don't remember when this was exactly, the Municipal Assembly started to operate again as an official body, and Mr. Stakic was the speaker of the assembly, the chairman who carried out the decisions of that body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What was the real function of Dr. Stakic, a more representing function or the real leader at that time, in 1992, especially after the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the 30th of April, 1992, Dr. Stakic discharged the functions of the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. From that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. time on, depending on the period in question, he was president of the Serbian Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And as we noted before, depending on the decisions of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, he was president of the Crisis Staff or the president of the War Presidency, and later president of the Municipal Assembly. After that, new elections were held, and he was replaced by another man as president of the municipality. And Mr. Stakic was later again elected president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor for another four-year term. This, as I said, is the supreme legislative body in the municipality which passes laws, enactments, conclusions by voting in accordance with democratic principles. And he is the president. The president is required to obey the decisions of the assembly, and if the decisions of the assembly are promulgated in Official Gazettes, for instance, he signs them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you regard Dr. Stakic as a strong politician or, as it is sometimes in politics, compromise candidate? What was your impression when you saw first Dr. Stakic the 7th of January, and then later in his acting capacity, especially at this meeting you mentioned the 29th of April when you were called together, and you found out together the time is ripe now for the takeover? Was Dr. Stakic a figure of leadership or puppet on the string of somebody else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know Dr. Stakic very well. He's much younger than me, so I did not have any contacts with him prior to that. He was a physician. As a person, I believe that he does have integrity, that he is firm, he's educated, he's smart. As far as politics are concerned, I believe that he was both at the same time, that he was firm in his decisions and in the implementation of the decisions of the Municipal Assembly, and I also assume that as a humanitarian, that is, as a person who belonged to the medical profession, he encounter situations in which he had to listen to people's problems and show leniency at times in order to help towards solving certain problems. I don't know whether he was a puppet. I wouldn't say that, but I would say that he was under the influence of the late Kovacevic and Simo Drljaca. However, even if there had been influences or pressures, I never heard of them or I never witnessed them in any of the official meetings that I rarely attended. I repeat that. So these influences and these pressures were never visible or officially exerted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I confront you with a quote from an interview given by Dr. Milomir Stakic later on when looking back to these events, he stated, page 2 of the transcript of Document S187-1C: "These places, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, were a necessity in a given moment and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor." Please comment this sentence.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not attend a single meeting at which such a decision would have been passed. Maybe Dr. Stakic had in mind major problems that had occurred, and the situation of war that prevailed in town and the things that happened on the 22nd and the 29th, and the army went into a mopping-up operation around Hambarine and Kozarac. And this was a necessary evil. A number of Muslims did create problems and committed crimes, shot at people. On the 16th and during the mopping-up operations in Kozarac and Hambarine and later on. So I assume there was a need for these people to be brought in and interviewed. Maybe there were justified reasons for the existence of Omarska and Keraterm. As far as Trnopolje is concerned, I've already told you when the combat activities started, people of their own will sought shelter from the fighting and went there. Two men were there who were carrying out orders in Prijedor, the late Kovacevic and late Drljaca called me on the phone. And we were on a conference call, so I could hear both of them talking at the same time, and they pressurised me into assuming that role. I was already 50 at the time. I enjoyed certain reputation. People liked me. I am a native of Prijedor. Actually, I've lived in Prijedor since the age of 3. I was born in Serbia, but I was born to a family of refugees from Prijedor who went to Serbia during the Second World War. So they asked me, they ordered me to go there to receive these people. I went up there, and I saw for myself that this was a huge misfortune that up to then, I could only see on television and in films, similar to things that are now happening in Iraq where people are fleeing in huge numbers in order to save their hide. People were coming there in huge numbers on foot, and I tried to help them, to find accommodation. So it didn't take me long to decide, because that's the kind of person I am. I decided to take that role to help these people, to receive them. And in conclusion, let me say that maybe Dr. Stakic -- maybe this is what Dr. Stakic thought, but I personally never attended a meeting at which it was decided to set up any of the three forms or three places where people would gather. But let me tell you, Trnopolje is something completely different because it was never a prison or a camp. It was never an investigation centre or interrogation centre or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me quote once again and little bit longer: "These places such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje were a necessity in a given moment and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor. Reporter: So those three camps or how are they? Stakic: Reception centres. Reporter: Reception centres were formed according to your civilian authorities. Stakic: Yes. Yes. As I have said, this was a necessity in the given moment when there was no longer any possibility to resolve the question of relations and the division of power through agreement by peaceful means and to an extremist from the ranks of the SDA, Party of Democratic Action and the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union Party, but mostly the SDA which won here and which at one point lost control and started using force, murdering members the army and the police. We had to set up such centres."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept this as an explanation, however, I don't know. I never heard of any formal civilian body taking a decision to set up these centres. At least, not Keraterm and Omarska. And as far as Trnopolje is concerned, I have already told you how this decision was taken and how this was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You told us how it was established. I would ask you, who ran Trnopolje centre, what would be your answer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say because this was not either a classical camp or any firm organisation. It was an open centre, and it would be the most logical thing to say that it was run by the Red Cross from Prijedor with huge assistance by the Red Cross from Banja Luka and UNHCR. I was the one who organised and provided for the security of these people through the military command. And as for the supplies and food, this was done via the Red Cross, via the Municipal Assembly, and with the assistance of the institutions that I mentioned earlier on. That is, the Red Cross and the UNHCR. So there was no classical command, nor was there any need for such a command. When people came there, I could not prevent anybody from entering, nor could I prevent anybody from leaving. There were cases when people came and wanted to take people away. I wanted this to be recorded, because I wanted to prevent situations where an accident would happen to these people, and later on nobody would know what had happened to these people, who had taken them away. That's why I wanted all these instances recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, how would you describe your relationship with Dr. Stakic in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic was the president of the Municipal Assembly i.e., the bodies that I've already mentioned. In our private life, we didn't socialise because he is much younger than me. He has his own friends, people he socialised with. I personally did not socialise with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did he exercise his duties in a professional Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. manner?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that he did. He exercised duties for which he was appointed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: What about the reasons that led to the fact that the first representatives in Prijedor at the same time left their posts in the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what this is all about and what representatives you're talking about. I don't remember. I can't place that in time. I don't know who left their posts. But I believe that there were elections, weren't there? And that a new assembly was established. Now whether that was in 1993 or 1994, I don't know exactly. I only know that there were new multiparty elections, that is, the elections for the representatives to the Municipal Assembly, and the new president of the Municipal Assembly was elected. I don't know whether this was in 1993 or 1994. I don't remember. I can't recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Quite concrete: Why had Dr. Stakic to leave his office or his post as president of the Municipal Assembly without any elections beforehand in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. You've taken me by surprise. Maybe he resigned or something like that. I really honest to God do not remember. I believe that Dr. Stakic had a vice-president. He was Dragan Savanovic, and I believe that he was succeeded by a dark-haired, tall guy. I can't remember his name. Oh, it was Dusan Kurnoga. I believe that was his name, Dusan Kurnoga. But whether he replaced Dr. Stakic or whether he was elected and appointed when the new assembly was elected, I don't know. I don't think he would just replace him just like that. And my logic tells me that if Dr. Stakic had resigned for some other reasons, then he should have been replaced by his vice-president. And that was Mr. Dragan Savanovic. Whether this happened or not, honest to God, I can't remember at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One final question: Already yesterday we discussed the replacement of Professor Cehajic during the takeover. And apparently he was on a list prohibiting him to enter his office as a freely elected president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Did you follow what happened to Professor Cehajic? What about the fate of Professor Cehajic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you have just stated is correct. It was a fact that he was not allowed entrance. What happened to him later on, I don't -- I didn't know at that time. After a few days, I believe he was taken first to Keraterm and then to Omarska, but I don't know after how many days that was. I don't know whether something happened to him that would be relative to the risk of his life. There were rumours all over town that somebody got killed, somebody didn't. And later on, those people who were rumoured to have been killed would return -- would appear in Prijedor. Many people of Muslim and Croat ethnicities returned to Prijedor in 1994, 1995, 1996. These same people had been rumoured to have been killed, so I really don't know what happened with Professor Cehajic. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Professor Cehajic after the 30th of April 1992 again?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know for a fact. I believe that I saw him once somewhere in town, but I'm not sure. I can't remember. I believe that I saw him, but I can't remember where and why. At the time when he was incarcerated or taken for interrogation, and after that time, I never saw him again. I didn't even see him on the 30th of April when he turned up for work. I only heard that the policemen stopped him and others who to be replaced by new members of the Executive Board, and they had to return to their homes. And when that happened, when Professor Cehajic was either arrested or taken for interrogation, I don't know. I only know that the person who talked to him was Simo Miskovic, or maybe representative Srdic. I believe that one of them talked to him on that day, either on the 30th of April or the 1st of May. They talked to him on the telephone from the private house that had been rented by this Slovenian company. And I believe that they said that Professor Cehajic was in Ljubija staying with his sister or somebody. And I believe that Mr. Senator -- a senator talked to him. I don't know what they talked about. I assume that Mr. Cehajic had said that what had been done was not okay, and then the gentleman who spoke to him explained, then gave the justification for that. And he explained that by the thing that had been taking place before the takeover. But in any case I really -- I cannot remember exactly what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would you know about any crime Professor Cehajic allegedly had committed justifying his incarceration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer your question because I'm not a lawyer by profession, and I've never been engaged in a job similar to yours, Your Honour. I can only say that he was a member of the SDA, that together with Mr. Mirza Mujadzic, he organised the armament of the Muslim people, especially in the area around Hambarine. He helped in the arming of paramilitary formations together with him, based on what I could read in the newspapers and hear on the radio, and based on the statements of other people from other parties, he was the one who obstructed the establishment of the legal authorities in the executive branches of power. So maybe somebody decided that this was a good enough reason to incarcerate him. But personally, I would not find that a justifiable reason. The only thing that I would find a justifiable reason would be the armament of illegal paramilitary formations. That was a different matter. Mr. Cehajic was the president of the Municipal Assembly, and most of the power was in the hands of the SDA. So there was no need to -- for them to arm themselves. Maybe the leaders of the party spoke differently and ordered people differently. I know that Muslim people sold their property in order to obtain arms, but that's a different story. This is something you didn't ask me, did you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please, once again, try to concentrate on the question and answer to the best of your recollection. How many days was it from the 30th of April, 1992, until the day of his incarceration? One day, two days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I really can't assist you with that. But I don't believe that he -- that it happened so quickly. I don't remember. Immediately after the 30th of April, these things didn't happen. All these problems and incarceration of people took place after the 22nd or the 26th of May. I don't know whether I'm right in saying that. I really can't remember, and it wouldn't be fair of me to say things that I don't know for a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Absolutely correct. You should only tell us what you know for sure. But Mr. Kuruzovic, isn't it true that you know that Professor Cehajic, in fact, died in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that for a fact. I heard it like I heard of some other citizens of Prijedor, unfortunately. I heard it in conversations with people, because nothing has ever been said officially by any of the bodies. We've never read about it in any of the newspapers. We never heard it on any of the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This, in principle, concludes my line of questions. And out of order, because I don't know what it's about, may I ask the usher to present a document that has not yet an exhibit number. Please put it on the ELMO. Would you please be so kind and tell us what kind of document this is.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not a document. This is what we call an accompanying letter which accompanies a different document which is either an order or a decision. This is a piece of paper which confirms the delivery of the decision of me being relieved of my duties of the commander of the territorial staff of Prijedor. I don't see a signature here. Probably I did sign this document, because it confirmed the fact that I received the decision on my relief of duties. This was a decision that must have been taken earlier on, but administratively, it was delivered on the 30th. I believe it was taken on the 29th or thereabouts. I don't know. Here, I can actually see the date, 29th is the date. And it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. delivered to me on the 31st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
