utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, isn't it true that principal political decisions on the most important issues were initially taken by had the SDS leadership, and later on these decisions were implemented by the civilian, police, military bodies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree with you. At that time, when the power was taken over and Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was officially established, this was a so-called monoparty system. There was the Serbian Democratic Party, and all the people who were appointed to various positions were members of the Serbian Democratic Party. Like everywhere else in the world, they were supposed to implement the policies of the Serbian Democratic Party, and I hope I have answered your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So is it true that a person couldn't be appointed to an important post without prior recommendation of SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now, the highest positions in the republic and in the larger towns and towns like ours, I really don't believe that anybody could have been appointed if they were not members of the Serbian Democratic Party. Maybe members of the Executive Board or managers or CEOs or directors of institutions could have been appointed without even being Serbs, let alone members of the SDS. At the beginning, it was a widespread thing. But later on, as things moved on, it was only Serbs that were appointed, and that is, members of the SDS. In the meantime, things have again changed. A lot of people have returned. The president of our municipality again is a Muslim, and there are a lot of other posts in the municipality and other institutions taken by both Muslims and Croats who are not members of any party. For example, the president of the Municipal Assembly is a member of the party for Bosnia-Herzegovina, but others are not. But still, things do follow party lines. In the past, there was just one party. Now, there are several parties. But people are appointed from parties, from various parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, who did belong to the SDS leadership in Prijedor Municipality in 1991, 1992? Please do name the most influential political figures in the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were president of the municipal board of the SDS, Mr. Simo Miskovic; vice-president of the party, Dragan Savanovic; and other members of this municipal board who had more or less influence. Since we are talking here about something that has to do with Mr. Stakic, he as a humane person and as a doctor had a certain renown. And even before he was elected president of the municipality, I don't think he had much influence along party lines. Our municipality consists of a large number of local communes. Dr. Stakic did work in Prijedor, but originally he comes from a local commune that used to be a municipality in its own right before the war. And it was necessary for that part of the municipality to be represented in the government because other offices were filled by people from other parts of the municipality. So he was elected as a representative of the Omarska local commune, which used to be a municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... to my question, but you didn't explain why Dr. Stakic, being -- having no much influence as you said, was elected president of Serbian Assembly in January of 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I hoped I had explained because he was from an area of the municipality with a large population, and where I come from, we take great care to ensure equal representation. And this large population had to be represented in the municipal, legislative body. He was elected because he was a well-respected man, a doctor, well-known, and this population elected him and made him their deputy. There was a voting ballot listing the names of nominees for various functions, such as president, vice-president of the municipality, and other posts. And he was voted -- he got the most votes. That's how he was elected president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, whom Dr. Stakic was subordinated to before the takeover and after the takeover? As I understand, before the takeover, Dr. Stakic has dual status. On the one hand, he was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly; and on the other hand, he was president of Serbian Assembly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But as a president of Serbian Assembly, whom he was subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in terms of subordination, you could say he was subordinated to the Assembly of Krajina. But this was just form. I don't know how to explain it to you better. It wasn't the practice in real life. You know that he could have been regarded as vice-president of some sort of shadow government, but it wasn't a real shadow government. The assembly's legislative body and the government is an executive body. It was pure form. Serbian people said that they were establishing their own Serbian Republic. They wanted their own Serbian government, their own president, their own assembly, their own Executive Boards and so on and so forth. So that on the 29th and the 30th of May, none of that actually functioned. It was just an expression, a formal expression of the will of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Can you name the persons, the politicians, whom Dr. Stakic contacted and who were among the leadership of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Krajina? I don't know that. If you're talking about Serbian Krajina, you mean Knin? I don't know which time you are referring to. I don't know whether he had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Referring to before the takeover, the period before the takeover when Dr. Stakic was president of Serbian Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vice-president.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... he was president of Serbian Municipal Assembly since 7th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I don't know in which way and what was the formal and real reason that he contacted somebody from the Serbian Krajina, if he did. I told you it was just a formal expression of the will of the Serbian people. Throughout that time, I was the headmaster of a school. I didn't have any particular contact with Mr. Stakic from my job. If something needed to be resolved at the school, I would contact somebody in the Executive Board who was in charge of education matters. I didn't contact Stakic, so I don't know who he contacted in the Serbian Krajina. Maybe he did have a contact person there, but I neither heard about it nor witnessed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: After the takeover, the Crisis Staff of Prijedor Municipality became the only official body in Prijedor Municipality. Who -- whom was Dr. Stakic subordinated to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. There was the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. That is distinct from the Serbian Krajina. As far as I can remember, I think the president of the Crisis Staff of that Autonomous Region of Krajina was Mr. Brdjanin. He was either president of the assembly or president of the Crisis Staff, or maybe Vojo Kupresanin was president of the assembly. In any case, it was one of the two. And according to the principles of subordination, I believe that person was above Dr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And what about Biljana Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mrs. Biljana Plavsic was president of the republic, and regardless of the fact that this ministate of ours was really small, she was far away, far removed from Dr. Stakic. As far as I remember, Mrs. Plavsic visited Prijedor only once, and I remember on that occasion she did speak to Dr. Stakic because he, as the holder of his office, had the duty of receiving her and talking to her. I don't know whether they had known each other before that. I don't think so. Mrs. Plavsic was a personality that far surpassed our municipal level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, in 1992, you were principal of the school. Yes? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: What was the normal duration of the academic year at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is prescribed by law. The school year begins on the first Monday in September and lasts for 37 weeks. One term is 18 weeks, and the other term is 19 weeks. So it ends on the -- between the 1st and the 10th of June the following year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you recall that the Crisis Staff decided to shorten academic year in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had forgotten about that, but I think that's true. That happened, I think, when the military action, or rather the incident in Hambarine happened, when this attack was mounted on Prijedor. I think classes were interrupted and did not continue that year. Normally, they should have lasted until June. I think the decision was made then to discontinue the school year. I'm not quite certain, but I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: It was on 20th of May. The Crisis Staff took this decision on the 20th of May. And why? Hostilities started on 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date, but I believe it's the date you quoted. I don't see what the reason could have been. I don't think it was linked with anything else. I don't know exactly what you're driving at. A lot of the teachers were on the front line, but they were substituted by their female colleagues. I really don't remember the reason why this decision was made. But if the Municipal Assembly or the Crisis Staff made that decision, the schools were required to comply without any comment. That's all I can remember. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you know that at that time, the work obligations were introduced in Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say one way or another, but I suppose that yes, if that was introduced, it must have been governed by the decisions of the Secretariat for National Defence. Because they were in charge of men, and since there had been the takeover of power, movement was restricted for several days. There was a curfew from 10.00 p.m. to 6.00 a.m., and that helped preserve peace and quiet in town. Nothing much happened. Yes, I think you're right. I think the work obligation was indeed introduced then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Do you remember when the work obligations were introduced?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't remember. I can't give you a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: June?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. If the Crisis Staff made that decision, then it could only have been in May or in June. But if it was made earlier, then it was made by a different body. But I don't think it was earlier. I think we worked normal hours before. There was no state of emergency, because a Crisis Staff is formed, for instance, in case of a climactic natural disaster. For instance, a Crisis Staff was recently established in Prijedor because there was a danger of flood. It may sound nasty to you as a term "Crisis Staff," but that was a body that was supposed to deal with emergencies, and that's the term we used. So I am sorry, but I can't really tell you when the decision was adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuruzovic. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are welcome, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One follow-up question that we have it in the time coordinates, you just mentioned the visit of Ms. Biljana Plavsic to Prijedor. When was this, to the best of your recollection? Was it in summer or fall 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in autumn, but I can't remember exactly. I don't even know whether it was in 1992, but I suppose it was, sometime in autumn. Maybe even winter. I'm not sure really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Was it together with the visit of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I remember that Mrs. Plavsic, as vice-president of Republika Srpska, came alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Do you recall visits paid to Prijedor by Mr. Karadzic and/or Mr. Krajisnik in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they visited in 1992. At least, I don't know about Mr. Karadzic. But I know that he did come once, either in 1992 or 1993. He attended the ceremony of baptism of the church in Marini. I think that was the immediate reason why he visited Prijedor. I suppose that he also spoke with municipal leaders, the representatives of legislative and executive bodies and party leaders, but I didn't attend a single meeting together with Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wasn't there such a meeting in September/October 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. But I'm not certain. It seems to me it was in autumn, and I think the foundations of that church were then christened. As far as I know, that church was never completed to this day. There is no place for people to worship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Wasn't there a political meeting in a hotel Prijedor in September/October 1992 that was attended by in any event Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible, but I don't know. I didn't attend any such meeting. If Mr. Karadzic was there, I don't think such an occasion would have been missed. He, as head of Republika Srpska, must have addressed the people who gathered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Argibay, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I have a little confusion with the dates. Just correct me if I got something wrong, but you were elected the 7th January, 1992, as the head of the Serbian Territorial Defence unit, and you said that was at the time a sort of wish of the Serbian people, the Serbian citizens of Prijedor, but that body didn't work at that moment. And so you stayed as a principal to a school until the takeover in Prijedor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And after the takeover, when I was -- before I was a headmaster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: I'm coming to that. After the takeover, then this office, as the head of the Serbian Territorial Defence unit, was put into practice, that was real enough. You have these offices in Cirkin Polje or Urije and some staff under you until at least officially the 29th of May, that the decision was made to disband this territorial office and, you said, resubordinate you to the brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I was subordinated to the brigade as early as the 16th or 17th of May, and that was confirmed in writing by a decision that was delivered to me on the 31st and was dated the 29th. You are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So your office as the head of this Serbian Territorial Defence was practically functioning, let's say, from the 30th of April until the 16th of May, that is, 16 days. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. And that was the time when you were, for instance, issuing the vouchers for the petrol delivering, or were you doing another kind of task? And if so, which one?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did issue those petrol coupons, but I don't know how long that lasted, when that ended. A few days early -- one day, they came from the municipal Secretariat for the Economy and took over this job for me. Before that, I had a number of discussions of some renowned people, representatives of the Muslim and Croatian communities trying to reach an agreement with them to jointly preserve peace, law, and order in our town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: So after the 16th, 17th of May, you were resubordinated to the brigade, and you just leave the offices in -- I don't remember, it was Cirkin Polje or Urije, and I'm sorry for the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your pronunciation is very good. And in any case, I'm listening to the interpreter. You are right, Your Honour. From that moment on, I was no longer officially the commander of that staff. And then when the written decision came, the Territorial Defence or its staff also ceased to exist. Everything became subordinated to the brigade command. I don't know whether it happened on the 16th or the 18th or the 19th. The staff was restructured into some sort of logistics base, and they continue to discharge those parts of their functions which had to do with supplying army troops and the police manning checkpoints. As far as I remember, it was Mirko Mudrinic who was appointed commander of that logistics base.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Okay. Then I come to the next appointment you had, and I'm not very clear when was that. I seem to recall, and I don't have the transcript in front of me, that you said that Mr. Kovacevic and someone else were the ones who asked you to be sort of in charge of the Trnopolje camp. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is all correct, apart from the -- well, that is your opinion. I, for instance, would not subscribe to calling it a camp. As for the rest, you are right. This discussion I had with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: With?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular interview was held with me by late Mr. Drljaca and Dr. Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: And what was the date of that particular interview, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but it must have between the 20th -- sorry, 22nd and the 26th or the 27th perhaps. Because that attack in Hambarine happened on the 26th, and because of the counterattack of the army, people were fleeing their homes. And as far as I remember, they fled to the Mladost sports hall. I received a telephone call. Somebody from the municipality asked me to accommodate these people in the school building, and I declined. So these people spent a couple of days there because I didn't want to let them stay at the school. So that is about this school business. So the first call must have come between the 22nd and the 26th, and the second came on the 26th or the 27th when there was combat in Kozarac. It was a showdown between the people manning the checkpoint, some Muslims with the army. The Muslims were asked to surrender their weapons, and when they didn't, there ensued a clash. It is always the innocent people who are caught in the crossfire. And that is how it came about that people started fleeing their homes, and then I received this telephone call asking me to provide premises for them. I hope I answered your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes. But I have a clarification to ask. How was it possible that Mr. Kovacevic was at that time a member of the Crisis Staff because he was the president of the Executive Board, and Mr. Drljaca was the chief of the security station in Prijedor, and you were subordinated to the brigade? How is it possible that those two persons were able to, sort of, send you to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that before that, they had a conversation with Mr. Arsic. And I don't know. I didn't check it -- check that subsequently. It never occurred to me to ask. They called me as a person, as a citizen. But I was an officer at the time, but everybody over the age of 22 was a soldier. So there was no strict military subordination at the time. I assume that they got -- they did it in agreement with the army, but they didn't tell me that. They just asked me to do it, and when I went to Trnopolje, first I didn't accept that. But just as a private individual, I went there to see whether people were really coming there. And when I saw that, to my great regret, I accepted the position. But maybe it was God's will for me to go there because I'm a very sensitive person, and maybe this helped those people because nothing that happened there can be considered a disgrace for my people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry I have to interrupt you. But I learned just in this moment, the tape ran out. And we have to exchange the tapes. And therefore, we need a short break. Sorry that -- I know it's not a convenient moment. For technical reasons, the trial stays adjourned until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Once again, sorry for having interrupted you for technical reasons. If you want to add something to that what you stated previously, please feel free to do so.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add. I hope that the Honourable Judge was satisfied with my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. But I have, I hope, only one following up. That's you said that you suppose that Mr. Kovacevic, Dr. Kovacevic and Mr. Drljaca had spoken with -- I don't know if he was a colonel by that time or what, Mr. Arsic, beforehand, because you were subordinate to him. Does this mean that there was a constant coordination of conversations between the members of the Crisis Staff or the chief of the security station in Prijedor with the commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there was a constant coordination. This was an exceptional situation. Somebody had to be sent over there to receive all these people. I shared with you my assumption and why I believe that they insisted on me going there. As far as the army is concerned, at that particular moment, I did not have any military duties in the barracks or in the brigade. I don't know how all this happened, whether that was the commander's recommendation or whether it initially came as a request. But I believe it was a mutual agreement that a person like me - I feel embarrassed talking on my own behalf - but a person like me whom everybody knew and the two or three of them expected that I would look after these people well. And I suppose that they believed that I would not be a disgrace for my own people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't have any further questions, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So finally, if need may be, to whom would you report in 1992 in this capacity in Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in almost daily contact with the army command. This was customary in the units, to come for briefing every morning. And every morning, I would inform the commander about the unit which provided security on the previous day, and I would ask for a different unit to provide the security on that particular day. As far as the accommodation of these people was concerned and provisions for them, the provisions of food and water, the army had nothing whatsoever to do with that. If there was any need for any such of intervention there, I would contact Mr. Travar, who was the secretary for the economy with the Executive Board. And if I needed food or any such thing, I would turn to him. But there were not many such requests because we had permanent assistance from the Red Cross and the UNHCR who brought a lot of flour and milk for the children, and other types of food. Sometimes even fruit. Very often, we would get packed lunches from the local Red Cross. So there was no starvation, there were no outbreaks of illnesses. I've already said that. So the army had nothing whatsoever to do with anything else but provide for the security for this centre, for the people who would guard the centre from the possible attacks of Serbs. There were attacks, people who arrived from Prijedor would be attacked. Their bicycles and money would be taken away from them. And after that, a majority of people would arrive by train. That was safer. Every day, there were families coming from Prijedor and would stay there for a couple of hours. They would bring these people food. But I believe that I have already said all that. I don't want to waste your precious time in repeating myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You stated "I would inform the commander." Could you please also add a name.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of that unit was Arsic. I don't know whether he was colonel or lieutenant-colonel at that time. I believe that he was colonel. I would inform him about the unit who had performed the security duty on the previous day, and I would ask him for a new unit that would Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perform security duty on the following day. So there was always one duty, one unit on duty, and they would be there for 24 hours to safeguard these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So would the final conclusion be correct that you felt yourself in two hierarchies?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how other peoples felt, but I did, because I was charged with the care for these people. I had to be in constant contact with both the military authorities and the civilian authorities because there were problems. There were attacks. People got their property stolen from them, and that's why I had to turn to the military police. And I had to ask them to arrest some people, not only the people who came as far as Trnopolje and the people there, but also people in Kozarac and around Kozarac who looted property there. There are a lot of people up there. This is closer to Trnopolje, not across the Prijedor/Banja Luka Road towards Kozarac. People lived in their houses, and they heard and they knew I was looking after these people and that I made a lot of interventions to prevent such things from happening. So these people came straight to me to complain, and then I would turn to either the military or the civilian and ask them to regulate things over there. On one occasion, a delegation came into my centre. It was headed by the deputy Minister of Health, Mr. Cedo Aleksic. He brought a delegation and among those people was a congressman from the United States of America who after having visited the centre and the school, he asked to be introduced to the person called Kuruzovic. He was introduced to me, and he thanked me. He told me that he had heard from the people that I looked after them and after their security as much as I could, that I looked after their food and the -- and now, as to the conditions, whether these conditions were good or not is hard to say. One is obviously most comfortable at his own home, needless to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask finally, you were paid by whom at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was paid by the army at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. There was a difference between the salary of a military officer and the salary of a school principal, which was my original job. I've already said that I would leave that place in -- late in the afternoon because there was security there. But every morning around 8.00, I would be at school, and I would be paid for that as well. But at that time, the salary of an officer was higher than the salary of a principal, so I would receive not the whole salary but the difference between the salary of a principal and the salary of a military officer. I would receive that difference from the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. This concludes the line of questions by the Judges. It's only for us now to decide on this accompanying letter. It was given to us by the Defence. Is it tendered by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think that it explains when the actual decision was delivered to Mr. Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no objection. So the record is clear, I believe Your Honour was referring to the document shown to the witness, the last document shown to the witness, which had the ERN number stamp of 01119285. Also, Your Honour, we have a translation available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: There is no ERN number on this document, sorry to say this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. I see. Apparently we've added it since then. But we do have a translation of the document, if Your Honour would like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. As to the fact that there is no objection, and if it's in fact the same document, this would be then D124A and B respectively. And now, as mentioned beforehand, as to the fact that Mr. Kuruzovic appeared on the list of the Defence witness, it would be for the Defence to continue with the line of questions. Mr. Lukic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kuruzovic.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We already know each other, but just for the record, my name is Branko Lukic, and together with John Ostojic who is not here today, and Mr. Cirkovic, I represent Dr. Stakic's Defence team before this Tribunal. Also, to avoid any confusion, yesterday, it was mentioned that you were on the list of Defence witnesses. However, after this conversation with me, when you declined the possibility of being a Defence witness, as from that moment on, you are no longer on the list as a Defence witness, and that's why you were invited to give your testimony by the Chamber. Mr. Kuruzovic, I would like to clarify something with regard to a document that was shown to you earlier today, and I believe that we will have more opportunity to discuss documents tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to give you the document S276.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, can you tell from this decision which body passed the decision itself, that is, the decision on the closure of work of schools in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the session of the 20th of May, 1992, by the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. And this was the decision for the interruption of work of elementary and secondary schools in Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judge Vassylenko asked you how was it that the Crisis Staff issued the decision on the termination of work of schools in the territory of Prijedor? Does this decision mention the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will no longer need this document for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: To be correct, it mentions the president of the municipal, Dr. Milomir Stakic, as the signator. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me, then the answer is yes, it does say Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuruzovic, when you left the army, you were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the JNA, after the regular military service.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After that, you were promoted, and what was the highest rank that you were awarded?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the JNA army, it was captain first-class.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the regular military service, can you tell us what functions in the former JNA did you discharge as a noncommissioned officer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was from the commander of a platoon to the commander of a battalion. In the 11th Brigade, I was a company commander, and before that I was also a company commander in a battalion, and also in the 6th Sana Brigade, I was a battalion commander up to the year 1986 or thereabouts. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During your service in the army and later on when you were a member of the JNA as a noncommissioned officer, was it possible, did you ever witness that a lieutenant could issue an order or command somebody who had the rank of a major or a captain first-class?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible through the method of subordination. The army could resolve its own problems in different ways. For example, it could happen that a battalion or a company had a number of officers, and that one of the officers would be a higher ranking officer, but the other -- but he was also elderly, and he could not exercise his duties properly. And in that case, he could receive orders from somebody with a lower rank, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. but younger. There were such instances. I'm speaking from experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're talking about relationship between two officers. But is there a possibility that for a noncommissioned officer could issue orders to a captain?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that could not happen. Only if a captain was a member of a unit and if he was a commander of a company or of a platoon, in that case, the commander of a brigade or region or a corps could convey the order of a higher instance. But to issue a direct order, that was absolutely impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there a possibility for a foot soldier to order something to an officer? I know that this may sound silly to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does sound silly. But I suppose you know what you're doing, and therefore I won't object to your question. In life, everything is possible, but for a foot soldier to issue orders to an officer, that would be a very difficult thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Difficult or impossible?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Impossible. In the Second World War, we know who it was that issued orders to the entire German army, but since these units were composed of the ones that we're talking about, the units that existed in 1992, if you're talking about the JNA, then no, this is not possible. But if we're talking about some other units, then it would be possible because these units were composed of armed Serbian people, neighbours, friends, acquaintances, and maybe it was possible that somebody with a lower rank or without a rank would -- could be in a commanding position. For example, a commander of a platoon or a company. But that would not be a large unit. Maybe that would be only because he enjoyed respect. But in the proper military subordination, for a foot soldier to issue order to an officer, that would be unheard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Prijedor Municipality, did you ever witness a situation in which somebody who would -- who was a foot soldier, regardless of his reputation, would issue an order to Arsic or Zeljaja?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never witnessed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever witness a situation in which somebody who was not even a foot soldier, that is, a civilian, would issue a command to either Arsic or Zeljaja in the territory of Prijedor Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on all the documents that I have had the opportunity to see today, because they were presented to me by the Honourable Chamber, I saw decisions. But a civilian in any position or in any post, to have a possibility to issue an order to the commander of the region or the commander of a brigade, and for such an order to be implemented, I just don't believe that. The only orders that could be implemented by the commander of a brigade could come from the superior commander, that is, the corps commander. I'm talking about the orders and commands that deal with military issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were asked about the mobilisation that took place in 1991. Did all the men who responded to their callup receive weapons regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organisation of the Territorial Defence and its staff in the town of Prijedor at that time, in 1991, was such that there were regional staffs, regional staff in Urije, regional staff in Kozarac, which had under its command the company from Omarska. Then a regional staff in Prijedor I, Prijedor III, Celinci. In terms of territory, that's how it was divided. And the National Defence Council made a decision that members of the Territorial Defence should be mobilised by their respective staffs, and several days later, another decision was issued to arm them with infantry weapons. As for the question of Honourable Judge, the weaponry ranged from light rifles to light machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You probably know the ethnic composition of various places in the region.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that question. I have to rewind this film a little bit. For instance, the ethnic composition of Puharska and Donja Puharska was mostly Muslim. Of course, there were some Serbs. It was a multiethnic community with a majority Muslim population. Both communities were armed. In Hambarine --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is no need for us to go into that much detail. Just tell me, did all the men who responded to the callup receive weapons regardless of their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence, the staff headed by Mr. Javoric included some Muslim and Croatian staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several Croats and several Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992, did these people continue to come to work?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Along with the staff headed by Mr. Javoric, did they, too, join the 43rd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the staff was annexed to the brigade, I suppose they were, too. I know that some of them were there, Iso Bucan, Drago Motl. Drago Motl is a Croat. All this staff was attached to the command of the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you a document now, F4. And I would like to ask you something about the time when you were actually appointed commander of the Serbian Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Document S4.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since it's written in very short script, I'll read out a part of the text to you. The subject is: "Kozarski Vjesnik, issue dated the 24th of April, 1992." Subheading: "The political scene in Prijedor." And the heading is: "The elected government of the Serbian Assembly. The Municipal Assembly of Prijedor made a decision last week to merge the public auditing service of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality with the SDK of the Bosnian Krajina Autonomous Region in Banja Luka. At the 5th session of the Assembly of Prijedor, several important decisions were made. This primarily refers to the election of the government of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality and the decision to merge the SDK (the public auditing service of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality) with the SDK of the Bosnian Krajina autonomous region in Banja Luka." I made a break so that the interpretation can catch up. We continue: "In addition to the previously elected president of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The document that is shown on the screen starts with: "Several important decisions were made at the fifth session of the Assembly ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am reading from the original text. It's possible that interpreters are interpreting as opposed to reading from the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: This can't be true because as you're making reference to an article of the 24th of April, and then doesn't it read also in your text that this fifth session of the Assembly of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality, last Thursday, the 16th of April ..? We can't see it in the transcript. Therefore my question. Because I believe there's some importance about the fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 69, line 19 says: "At the fifth session of the assembly of Prijedor ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But here it continues: "Last Thursday, the 16th of April" and I think this is of utmost importance, that the Assembly of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality already assembled the fifth time the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We omitted the date accidentally before we found the text on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could please restart, we just heard that the interpreters didn't have the screen before them, and therefore omitted this "Thursday the 16th of April." Sorry. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start again, Mr. Kuruzovic. "Last Thursday (the 16th of April), at the fifth session of the Assembly of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality, several important decisions were made. This primarily refers to the election of the government of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality and the decision to merge the SDK (public auditing service of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality with the SDK of the Bosnian Krajina Autonomous Region in Banja Luka. In addition to the previously elected president of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality and chairman of the executive committee of the Prijedor Serbian Municipality, Milomir Stakic and Mico Kovacevic, the following persons were elected to the first government of this municipality: Bosko Mandic, to the post of deputy chairman of the executive committee;" and then the names go on until we reach line 10 of the second paragraph in this text where it says: Slobodan Kuruzovic as commander of the TO municipal staff. From this text, do you see that you were, in fact, not elected commander of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence on the 7th of January, 1991, but on the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything is possible. I was not a deputy to the assembly, but I was convinced that it was all done by the 7th of January. However, I see from this text that it was on the 16th of April. I've already told you my opinion, and this journalist here writes "government" and the executive committee is not a government. And it did not make decisions that related to the actual life of the entire municipality. Since I worked as headmaster at the time, it's possible that I confused the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, the difference between the two dates is more than three months, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How come that you don't remember exactly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to explain. I was involved and busy with my own job, and until the middle of April, none of these bodies really functioned in the municipality of Prijedor. Not until the 29th, the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There is a document about this on record with this Tribunal, and the number is 262, which testifies to the fact that these elections into the executive committee, or rather nominations for certain other posts, such as yours, took place on the 16th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that I confuse the dates. I was convinced that this had been done at the other session of the assembly. But here you are. I forgot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we now consider it as established that when you were giving your statement to this Court, you made a mistake, and the real date is, in fact, the 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can accept that, and I can say that it was a genuine mistake. It was simply an oversight. I sincerely believe that this decision had been made on the 7th of January. What really mattered to me is it was a decision of the assembly. The assembly was formally established on the 7th of January, and I thought they voted on these issues on the same day. But there you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't think there was any ill intention, but we need to clarify the dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So just that we need not come back to this point, it is still your testimony that the first meeting of this Serbian Assembly was held on orthodox Christmas, the 7th of January. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As we can read on this document, S4, speaking about the fifth session held the 16th of April, may I then ask, did you attend the meetings number 2, 3, and 4 of this Serbian Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not that I remember. I don't remember whether I was a deputy of that assembly or not. I was at one point a member of the assembly, but I don't know in which period. So many things happened at the time, and I don't recall assembly sessions by number. As for this session of the assembly that I attended, it was the one held on the 7th. And I must have attended this one, too, when I was nominated and put up for voting. It was the one on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. Mr. Lukic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kuruzovic, we heard testimony here about one man being elected on the 16th of April session without attending it.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean some other man?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, not you. Do you remember actually attending this session, or do you just suppose that you attended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I attended. I can't remember quite clearly. But when you said this a moment ago, I think you mean Slobodan Goronjic who was later appointed director of the SDK. I don't know whether it happened then or at some other time. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you and other citizens of Prijedor aware that before the takeover, military barracks and military convoys had been under attack in Croatia for a long time and weaponry was being seized from JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know at the time from the media that there were attacks on JNA columns in the Dobrovolacka Street in Sarajevo and in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time, in Prijedor, was it commonly believed that what was written in the communications from commanders of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Hasan Efendic, and the Minister of the Interior, Delimustafic, was a serious threat, the thing that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We established, and you told us yesterday, that your TO staff did not exist before the 29th of April, 1992. In fact, was not in operation.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did this staff cease to operate, in fact, on the 17th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, officially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to correct myself. 1992.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was transformed into a logistics base. I don't know whether it was a couple of days or less after the decision made by the Secretariat for the Economy. It was turned into the logistics base which had the job of meeting the needs of the army and the police and the crews manning checkpoints. I think it was Mirko Mudrinic who was at the head of this base.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know, or did you know at the time, that the Serbian Territorial Defence was abolished already on the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not officially aware of that, but I know that it was abolished and the that army of Republika Srpska was established. And the information that I received from the commander arrived either on the 16th or the 17th. Actually, it was the order to go there and to become a member of that army. Maybe it was -- the decision was taken earlier on, maybe in the ministry that the Territorial Defence would be established. And pursuant to that, the commander gave me my order to resubordinate myself to that army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please don't testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to save some time. Could the witness please be shown the document S141, please, page 44 in B/C/S or 59 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the top of page 44, you will find the name of Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's page 59, the last paragraph, English version, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the minutes of the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People, Bosnia-Herzegovina, held on 12 May, 1992, in Banja Luka. If you turn to the following page, it's going to be page 45 -- are you now on page 44?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm on 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It says: "Participated in the discussion at the session held on 12 May, 1992, a law was passed on the amendments of the Law of National Defence. Article 1 in the National Defence Act, Official Gazette number 4/92 of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in all provisions of the act, the terms `Territorial Defence' and `armed forces' shall be replaced by the following words: `The Serbian Republic of BH army.' "Article 2, subsection 2 of Article 10 is hereby expunged: It is an article in a subsection which regulated something concerning Territorial Defence. Article 3, articles 37 to 53 also all have to do with Territorial Defence and are hereby expunged. Article 4, this act shall enter into effect eight days from its publication in the Official Gazette of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Mr. Kuruzovic, can you tell from this document that the Serbian Territorial Defence was abolished on the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that. It was published in the Official Gazette which has to be done within eight days, and then I received my order to resubordinate myself to the regional command, and I received that on either the 16th or on the 17th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll no longer need this document. [In English] But I would like the usher to show the witness Document Number S113, please, if we have time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: One more document, and then please conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document, page 66 from the Official Gazette issue 2/92, this is a conclusion dated 29 May, 1992. At its meeting of 29 May, 1992, Prijedor municipal Crisis Staff reached the following conclusion: "Because of the formation of the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the need for the Serbian Territorial Defence has ceased. The Serbian Territorial Defence shall be incorporated into the structure of the region and placed under its command." Mr. Kuruzovic, is this the decision of the Crisis Staff after which you no longer attended the Crisis Staff sessions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the decision of the Crisis Staff. I stopped coming to its session after the 16th of May. And pursuant to this conclusion of the Crisis Staff, I received my decision on being dissolved from my duties. And as for the other decisions, the Territorial Defence stopped existing, and I had to resubordinate myself to the region commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: One more question, because we are through for the day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, just a slight correction. We have before us page 69, and not 66 as reflected on the transcript. Issue number 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have the B/C/S version in front of me, and it's slightly nonreadable. So thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment, Mr. Kuruzovic, on the 29th of May, 1992, the Territorial Defence of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was it already abolished at that moment as we have seen in the document produced at the session of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN KURUZOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was abolished by the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic, and it came into effect, as it says there, eight days upon its publication in the Official Gazette of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then this was a consequence of that decision. The Crisis Staff issued its conclusion, and based on that, I received my decision. On the 29th May, in Prijedor, there was officially neither the staff of the Territorial Defence nor its commander. Pursuant to the decision of the Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Territorial Defence stopped existing eight days upon the publication of that decision in the Official Gazette. And that was applicable not only to Prijedor, but to the entire territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will continue today -- tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Tomorrow, once again in Courtroom I from 9.00 to 12.30, and then from 2.00 to 4.30. The trial stays adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 28th day of March, 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 25
